title: Medical Record Retrieval Cost for Law Firms: Fees, Models, Math
summary: What a law firm pays to retrieve medical records: provider copy fees, vendor pricing models, staff time and delay, with the math for a six-provider case.
body_markdown:
Most firms price record retrieval by looking at one number: the vendor’s fee per request. That number is the smallest part of the bill.


A typical personal injury file has five to eight providers. Each one charges its own copy fee. Someone at your firm spends hours finding custodians and chasing follow-ups. And every week the records sit unrequested is a week the demand cannot go out.


This guide breaks retrieval cost into its four parts, compares the pricing models vendors use, and works the math for a real six-provider case. If you are still choosing a vendor, our[comparison of 10 medical record retrieval companies](https://www.inquery.ai/post/best-medical-record-retrieval-companies-law-firms/) covers turnaround and deliverables side by side.


## The Four Costs Inside Every Records Request


Retrieval cost has four parts, and only two of them show up on an invoice.


### Provider Copy Fees


The provider charges for producing the records. State law sets the ceiling, and the ceiling depends on who is asking. Paper copies, electronic copies, imaging and billing ledgers can each carry a different rate.


### Vendor Fees


If you outsource, the vendor charges for the work of requesting and following up. This is the number most firms compare. Some vendors pass provider fees through at cost. Others fold them into a bundled price or add a handling markup.


### Staff Time


In-house retrieval costs paralegal hours. Even outsourced retrieval costs some, because staff still answer vendor questions, fix rejected authorizations and check what came back.


### Delay


Records that arrive late push the demand back. A demand that goes out a month later settles a month later, and that month has a carrying cost for the firm.


## What Providers Can Charge an Attorney


Copy fees for attorney requests are set by state law, not by HIPAA. That distinction catches a lot of firms.


### The HIPAA Fee Limit Covers Patients, Not Attorneys


Under[45 CFR 164.524](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/subtitle-A/subchapter-C/part-164/subpart-E/section-164.524) , a provider may charge a patient only a reasonable, cost-based fee for their own records. That limit applies when the patient exercises their right of access.


A request from your firm under a signed authorization is a third-party disclosure. In *Ciox Health v. Azar* (D.D.C. 2020), the court vacated HHS’s attempt to extend the patient fee limit to records sent to third parties at a patient’s direction. So when your firm requests records, state fee schedules govern the charge.


### State Rules Vary Widely


A few examples show the spread.


- **California:**[Evidence Code section 1158](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EVID&sectionNum=1158) lets a provider charge a pre-suit attorney $0.10 per page plus clerical time at up to $16 per hour. The provider has five days to make the records available.
- **New York:**[Public Health Law section 18](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/PBH/18) caps paper copies at $0.75 per page and bars a provider from denying access solely because of inability to pay.
- **Elsewhere:** many states allow a flat search or retrieval fee on top of a per-page rate, and the per-page rate often drops after the first 20 to 50 pages.


For a full state-by-state table, the[LlamaLab fee guide](https://www.llamalab.ai/blog/medical-record-fees-by-state-2026) and[Tavrn’s cost breakdown](https://www.tavrn.ai/blog/medical-record-retrieval-costs) both list statutory citations. Check the statute itself before you rely on any figure, because schedules adjust.


### Fees That Surprise Firms


The per-page rate is rarely the whole charge. Watch for these.


Fee When it appears How to limit it


Search or retrieval fee Charged per request in many states, even for a short chart Combine records and bills into one request where the provider allows it


Certification fee When you need a records affidavit for trial Ask for certification only on files likely to be tried


Imaging media Films and DICOM discs priced separately Request the radiology report first and media only if needed


Prepayment invoice Provider holds records until a fee is paid Use a vendor that pays provider invoices directly


Rush fee Expedited release Request early so rush is never needed


## The Three Pricing Models Retrieval Vendors Use


Vendors price retrieval in one of three ways. Each one shifts risk to a different place.


### Per-Request or Per-Provider Pricing


You pay a fixed fee for each provider you request. This is the easiest model to forecast per case. Published examples run from $20 per provider (our limited-time intro rate; the standard rate is $40) to[$50 per request at Record Grabber](https://recordgrabber.com/pricing.php) .


The question to ask is what counts as one request. Some vendors bill a resubmission after a rejection as a new request. Others bill records and bills from the same provider as two.


### Monthly Subscription


You pay a monthly fee for software and run requests yourself.[Arctrieval](https://www.arctrieval.com/pricing) publishes plans from $279 per month plus a $339 one-time fee, with no per-request charge. Your staff still does the chasing. The cost per request falls as volume rises, but staff time does not.


### Custom Quotes


Large litigation-support networks usually quote per engagement. Pricing may include per-page charges, minimums, rush fees or bundled services such as depositions. Ask for a written quote on a sample case before comparing.

## Records and Bills Cost Differently


A complete file needs two things from each provider: the clinical records and the itemized bill. They often come from different departments.


### Why Bills Are a Separate Request


Hospitals commonly route medical records through health information management and bills through patient financial services. Each department has its own fax line, its own form and sometimes its own fee. A request that reaches only one department returns half a file.


Firms feel this at the demand stage. The chronology is done, but the specials cannot be totaled because two ledgers are missing. Our[guide to medical summaries and damage specials](https://www.inquery.ai/post/medical-summaries-damage-specials-ai-personal-injury/) shows why the billing half matters as much as the clinical half.


### Billing Groups and Outside Billers


Large physician groups often bill through a separate company. That billing company may sit in another state and keep its own records. Finding it is part of the retrieval job, and it is easy to miss.


Ask any vendor how they handle this. If records and bills from one provider count as two requests, your per-case cost can nearly double. If the vendor finds the billing entity for you, that is staff time you never spend.


### Imaging and Pharmacy


Radiology reports usually come with the chart. Films and discs are a separate request with a separate media charge.


Pharmacy records are cheap but easy to forget. They often show treatment that never appears anywhere else in the file.


## The Hidden Cost: Paralegal Hours


Retrieval is mostly follow-up. The first request takes minutes. The calls, refaxes and corrected authorizations that follow take hours.


### Where the Time Goes


A single provider can require several distinct tasks.


- Finding the right records custodian and fax number.
- Learning the facility’s own authorization form or ID requirements.
- Resubmitting after a rejection for a missing date or signature.
- Calling every week until the file ships.
- Checking that records and bills both arrived and cover the full treatment period.


### Pricing Staff Time Honestly


Put a number on it. If a paralegal spends three hours per provider across a case and costs your firm $35 an hour fully loaded, retrieval costs about $105 per provider in staff time alone. That is more than any published vendor fee above.


Your numbers will differ. The point is to count them, because staff time is the cost that never appears on an invoice. Our[guide to how retrieval works](https://www.inquery.ai/post/ai-medical-record-retrieval-software-law-firms/) walks through each step in more detail.


## The Cost of Delay


Delay is the largest cost and the hardest to see.


A PILMMA benchmark[cited by Tavrn](https://www.tavrn.ai/blog/medical-record-retrieval-companies-for-lawyers) targets every record requested and received within 35 days. Many firms run well past that. Every week of delay pushes the demand, the negotiation and the fee back by a week.


Incomplete files cost even more. A demand built on records from four of six providers undervalues the case, and the missing providers often surface only after the offer comes in. That is why provider discovery matters as much as speed. Our[gap analysis guide](https://www.inquery.ai/post/ai-medical-records-gap-analysis-personal-injury/) covers how to find the providers a client forgot to mention.


## Worked Example: A Six-Provider Case


Here is the math for a typical motor-vehicle case with six providers: an ER, an urgent care, imaging, an orthopedist, a physical therapy clinic and a pharmacy.


Cost line In-house Self-serve portal ($50/request) Done for you ($20 intro / $40 standard per provider)


Vendor fees $0 $300 $120 intro / $240 standard


Provider copy fees Paid by firm Usually passed through Usually passed through


Staff time (3 hrs/provider at $35) $630 About $315 (half the follow-up remains) Close to $0 beyond review


Rejection rework Staff absorbs it Often billed as a new request Handled by the vendor


Total before copy fees About $630 About $615 $120 to $240 plus review time


The staff-time assumptions are illustrative. Swap in your own hourly cost and the hours your team actually logs. The gap between models usually holds anyway, because staff time dominates every scenario where your own people do the chasing.


## How to Compare Retrieval Quotes


Put every quote on the same basis before you compare. These questions surface most hidden costs.


### Questions About Price


- Is the fee per provider, per request or per page?
- Does a rejected and resubmitted request bill twice?
- Are records and bills from one provider one charge or two?
- Are provider copy fees passed through at cost or marked up?


### Questions About Work


- Who finds providers the client did not list?
- Who calls the facility when a request stalls?
- What exactly does your team need to supply, and when?


### Questions About Results


- What is the typical turnaround, and how is it measured?
- Do records arrive sorted, with missing items flagged?
- Can you see each request’s status without calling?

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How much does medical record retrieval cost per request?


Published vendor fees run from about $20 to $50 per provider request, before provider copy fees. Subscription software starts around $279 per month. Provider copy fees vary by state and record type.


### Does HIPAA cap what a provider can charge my law firm?


Usually not. The HIPAA cost-based fee limit applies to patients requesting their own records. Attorney requests under an authorization fall under state fee schedules.


### Who pays the provider’s copy fee?


The requesting firm pays it, often advancing it as a case cost. Many retrieval vendors pay the provider directly and pass the fee through, which keeps records from stalling on a prepayment invoice.


### Is outsourcing retrieval cheaper than doing it in-house?


For most firms, yes, once staff time is counted. At three hours per provider, in-house follow-up costs more than most per-provider vendor fees.
